work.title: Passion of Trophimus and Eucarpion (22 March)
work.edition: Machine translation (gpt-6.1-sol, Patristica, 2026-10-29) of: Codex Suprasliensis, ed. S. Severjanov (1904), CCMH transliteration (Corpus Cyrillo-Methodianum Helsingiense, Kielipankki), converted to Cyrillic; text boundaries from the TOROT/obdurodon text divisions (Syntacticus treebank data, commit 525cee4); 105r–107r

paragraphs.text: March 22. The martyrdom of Saints Trophimus and Eucarpion. There was great uproar and turmoil, beloved brothers, and the emperor was threatening God's servants fiercely. The governors everywhere were committing terrible evils and devising new and cruel tortures. There were

many rewards offered by the emperor, so that whoever found a Christian and handed him over would receive the rewards. And so, with every kind of harm and every kind of misery, everything everywhere was filled. But the Lord helped all who struggled to endure martyrdom, as happened with the glorious martyrs Trophimus and Eucarpion. These two holy martyrs were soldiers serving under the governor who tortured the Christians. He trusted no one else but these two in matters of torture, for they were cruel and inhuman, and they treated God's servants with the utmost cruelty. Trophimus and Eucarpion were sent to torture those called servants of God and to bind all who associated with them and shared the same faith. They went along devising bitter tortures. While they were thinking in this way, something like this happened, unknown to unbelievers and quite unknown even to believers. For a great fire, with a loud noise, kept sending out a voice in the air: “Where are you hastening, Trophimus and Eucarpion? Why are you threatening my servants? You will not overpower them or defeat them. Instead, you too will be with them, for I have thus shown you mercy.” Hearing this,

those two cruel, savage, and inhuman men fell to the ground, unable to bear either the sight or the voice. Kneeling down and covering their faces, they said, “Who is this great God who has appeared and spoken to us? We would be blessed if we were his servants.” As they said this in great fear, the fiery cloud split open and stood still, and a voice came from it, saying, “Rise and repent, and your sins will be forgiven.” When they had regained their composure, they rose with hope and saw someone in white robes sitting in the midst of the cloud, with many standing before him. Astonished at the sight, they said, “Receive us, Lord, as we give an account of the sins we have committed.” When they had said this, the cloud immediately vanished. These two wept and grieved over the great evil they had done. They prayed with tears, falling down and asking forgiveness for their sins. When they came near Nicomedia, those living in the city expected some harm to come from them to the Christians there. The two immediately went to the praetorium, that is, the court, where

the governor had ordered them to stay. But they forgot the purpose for which they had been sent. They remembered neither the emperor’s law nor his commands, but chose instead God’s law, which is salvation for soul and body. They entered the prison and immediately released those who were there, calling them brothers. They recounted the vision that had occurred and declared, “We too wish to become Christians.” To many this seemed an astonishing thing: Trophimus and Eucarpus, renowned for their cruelty and boldness, and sent by the governor to torture Christians, had disregarded the governor’s command and were instead helping the Christians. When the governor heard what had happened, he came to Nicomedia. He summoned them and said, “What has happened to you, you most wretched of all people? How have your resolute souls suddenly changed? Have you been poisoned? Tell me! Or have you lost your minds? Gather your wits and come to your senses, lest you suffer the very things you have so often done to others.” The two answered, “Because we did those things, we came to know the Lord, the true Word made known. We understood whom

we had done them to. We wish to be with those people; we long to live with them. [?] May you find men more cruel and inhuman, so that they may do the same things to us that were done to God’s servants, the confessors of the Christian faith. May we too be found worthy to be with them. In this way we answer for the sins we have committed.” When the two had said this, the governor ordered them to be beaten on their sides with rods and their wounds rubbed with haircloth. But he achieved nothing. He saw that they endured it gladly. Finally, having been defeated, he pronounced sentence on them: he ordered them to be consigned to the fire. The two courageously endured the wounds inflicted on them and were numbered among those who had suffered, together with the holy martyrs. They were found worthy to receive the kingdom of heaven. Thus the two holy martyrs of God died. In the city of Nicomedia. In Christ our Lord, with whom glory and power be to the Father. With the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
